paras: The threatened lynching in South Memphis took place on the night of September 6, 1903, when a Black man accused of attacking a woman in her Memphis home was captured and a mob formed against him. He broke away before police sent to protect him arrived, and a dispatch predicted that he would probably be lynched; no later report of his fate was found.

According to a Memphis dispatch, a man described as "a negro brute" broke into the home of Mrs. Nellie Straugh at 230 Pennsylvania avenue at about 3 a.m. on September 6. The dispatch said he tried to force her "into submission by choking her" until her infant of a few months began to cry, and that he then fled through the rear door.

That night the accused man was captured in South Memphis by persons the reports do not name. A call went to the police station for a detail of officers "to save him from a mob," but before the police reached the scene he broke away and escaped. The Memphis dispatch closed by stating that he would "probably be lynched some time during the night."
No report of a recapture, lynching, arrest or trial appears in the coverage, and the man's name was never printed.

The fullest account appeared on September 11 in The Commercial of Union City, Tennessee, which printed the Memphis dispatch with the accusation stated as fact, calling the attack "dastardly" and forecasting a lynching without comment. Outside the South the story ran as a New York Sun special under the headline "CHILD SAVE[D] HER," in The Minneapolis Journal on September 7 and in the Bemidji Daily Pioneer on September 9, where the dateline was reset. That version presented the event as a human-interest story about an infant frightening off an "assailant" and left out the mob and the lynching forecast.
The two versions differ mainly by omission: only the Memphis dispatch mentions the mob, and the Sun special printed the woman's first name as "Lellie."

bases: A Black man accused of an attempted assault was captured and a mob formed against him; police were sent for to save him and the dispatch predicted he would 'probably be lynched', a threatened lynching with no killing reported (A3).
The two versions (A1, A3) share their opening wording and derive from one Memphis dispatch; only A3 mentions the mob, and no local or follow-up report was found.
